title: Grace before meals
hook: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts

segments.voice: Yesterday, votive candles: a nurse lighting one after a night shift, and a flame that stays when she goes. Your line was the candle keeps praying. Who did you hold in the light? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

Tuesday night. Spaghetti, again. A seven-year-old has his fork halfway to his mouth when his grandmother clears her throat. He freezes, puts the fork down, and sighs. Everyone at the table makes the sign of the cross, some faster than others. Then, together, in about the time it takes the steam to rise off the plates, they say it. Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen. Fork back up. Someone asks for the parmesan. It's over so fast it's easy to miss what was just said. Today, those words, slowly.
screen: `A FORK HALFWAY UP.` → `A GRANDMOTHER CLEARS HER THROAT.` → `SAID IN THE TIME STEAM RISES.`

segments.voice: Here is the prayer, in a traditional English form: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." Four short phrases. Take them one at a time. First, bless us. Not the food first. The people. The ones at the table, tired, hungry, maybe annoyed with each other. The prayer starts by asking God to bless them. Second, these thy gifts. Thy gifts. The spaghetti was bought at a store, cooked by someone's tired hands, paid for with someone's work. All true. And the prayer still calls it a gift, from God, before it's anything else. That's today's line. It quietly rearranges the plate. Third, which we are about to receive. Receive, not take. A gift is received. You can't earn a gift; you can only accept it. And from thy bounty: from God's generosity, which is bigger than this meal. Fourth, through Christ our Lord. The prayer goes through Jesus, who did this himself. In Mark's Gospel, a huge hungry crowd has followed him into a deserted place, and the disciples want to send them away to buy food. Instead he takes five loaves and two fishes, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the loaves, and gives them to be shared. Everyone eats. Some readers see grace at the table as copying that gesture: look up, bless, then share. Some families add grace after meals too, a short thanks when the plates are empty. Before or after, the point is the same. The food was a gift.
screen: `BLESS US: THE PEOPLE FIRST.` · `THESE THY GIFTS.` · `RECEIVE, NOT TAKE.` · `HE LOOKED UP, BLESSED, AND BROKE.` · then, large: `FROM THY BOUNTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say grace before eating. Get ready now, for your next meal. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next thing you'll eat. A sandwich at a desk, a bowl of cereal, dinner with people you love. Picture the hands it passed through: the grower, the driver, the cook. Then picture yourself pausing for one breath before the first bite. If you pray, you can say the traditional grace, slowly, letting each phrase land: bless us, these thy gifts, from thy bounty. If you don't, just pause and notice where the food came from. The bell holds the time.
Grace before meals. A short blessing said at the table, asking God to bless the people and calling the food his gift. Today's word.
Your line: these thy gifts. Today, before every meal, even a snack, pause long enough to say grace, or at least one breath of thanks. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Catholic families make the sign of the cross and say the traditional grace, "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts," together before meals at home and sometimes in restaurants; some also say a grace after meals.

fork.setup: you're a disciple. a huge, hungry crowd has followed Jesus into a deserted place and it's late. you tell him to send them away to buy food. what does he do?
options: agrees, and sends them to the villages.
takes five loaves and two fishes, looks up, blesses, breaks and gives.
tells the crowd to fast until morning.
fork.reveal: he blesses what little there is, breaks it, and has it shared. everyone eats. grace at the table copies that gesture.

original.script: Benedic, Domine, nos et haec tua dona
original.say: beh-NEH-deek, DOH-mee-neh, nohs et hek TOO-ah DOH-nah
original.note: Latin: the traditional table grace, bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quick formula kids rush through before dinner.
what it means: four phrases that bless the people, call the food God's gift, receive it, and pray through Christ.
what a scholar hears: the Latin Benedic, Domine, nos et haec tua dona, echoing Jesus who looked up, blessed and broke the loaves (Mark 6:41).

sources.quoted: Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

notes: Mark 6:35–44 paraphrased: disciples suggest sending the crowd away to buy food; Jesus takes five loaves and two fishes, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks and gives. 'Five loaves and two fishes' is stated in the cited text.
Latin form 'Benedic, Domine, nos et haec tua dona quae de tua largitate sumus sumpturi, per Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.' Confirm wording and pronunciation; only the opening is used.
Grace after meals mentioned but not quoted.

Editor: 'the traditional English form Catholics use' (implies all Catholics) became 'a traditional English form'; 'Catholics who say grace are copying that gesture' is now framed as how some readers see it.
Catholic path day 1 also used this grace; this day takes it phrase by phrase rather than repeating that lesson's angle.
